newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Western donors lift Zambian aid squeeze-World Bank.
newsitem.headline: Western donors lift Zambian aid squeeze-World Bank.

text.p: Western donors on Friday lifted a year-long aid squeeze on Zambia and pledged a total of $435 million in aid to the country in 1997, the World Bank said.

"Zambia's external partners indicated plans to make available in 1997 at least $150 million in balance of payment support, plus an additional $285 million in project assistance," the World Bank said in a statement after a Consultative Group of donors meeting in Paris this week.

"Discussions are advanced between Zambia and its bilateral and multilateral partners on additional support to be provided in 1997 and 1998. Plans call for another Consultative Group meeting in late 1997," the bank added.
Western donors, led by the United States, reduced aid to Zambia in mid-1996 in protest against the manner in which general elections were held in November last year.
Seven opposition parties boycotted the elections after the Frederick Chiluba government amended the constitution to ban some candidates, including former president Kenneth Kaunda, from standing.
However, donor representatives at the Consultative Group meeting expressed satisfaction with the government's performance since the elections.

"Participants especially welcomed the government's efforts to strengthen governance institutions in Zambia. In particular, support was expressed for actions aimed at reinforcing the anti-corruption commission, electoral commission, drug enforcement commission and human rights commission," the World Bank said.
It said delegates were also pleased with assurances from the government that it would not introduce media controls as planned, and with the resumption of dialogue with opposition parties.
"Delegates urged that work begin immediately towards an early decision regarding Zambia's elgibility for the highly indebted poor countries debt relief initiative," the World Bank said.
Zambia's debt burden amounts to nearly 10 percent of its Gross Domestic Product.
The Chiluba government has been anxious to restore normal relations with donors, on which it is banking to fund one-third of its $1.1 billion 1997 budget.
According to finance minister Ronald Penza, Zambia requires around $200 million in balance of payment support and about $275 million in project aid this year.

Several human rights groups, including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch/Africa, said earlier this week they would lobby donors to maintain the aid squeeze on Zambia until the government improved its governance record.
